# The Museum of Almost Nothing

The museum has no sign, exactly. There is a brass plate by the door, though the letters have become difficult to read:

**THE MUSEUM OF ALMOST NOTHING**

Below that, in smaller print:

**Admission: one thing you were going to throw away.**

I discovered the place on an unremarkable Tuesday, while waiting for a bus that was thirteen minutes late. The museum stood between a locksmith’s shop and a small restaurant with a handwritten soup board. From the outside, it looked like one of those narrow buildings that contains either an architect’s studio, a storage room, or the private life of someone who does not wish to be disturbed.

Inside, it was a museum.

There were glass cases, handwritten labels, controlled lighting, and a wooden bench positioned at exactly the sort of angle intended to make a visitor feel that sitting down was part of the experience. The collection included a chipped bowl, a bus ticket, a stone that had been warm, an unsent letter, and several objects whose significance would become clear only after a while.

No object had belonged to anyone famous.

That was not, I think, an accident.

The collection was arranged not by century, material, or country of origin, but by proximity to the wastebasket. Everything here had nearly been thrown away.

A card near the entrance explained that the museum was open whenever the door was unlocked and that visitors should feel free to remain as long as they liked. There was no gift shop. There was no recorded announcement. A small note asked visitors not to try to improve the exhibits.

I had arrived intending to kill twenty minutes. Instead, I stayed for almost the entire afternoon.

## The Receipt

The first exhibit was a receipt.

It had been folded twice and bore a faint coffee ring near the bottom. The date was legible. The total was legible. Most of the merchant’s name had been worn away by friction.

The label said only this:

**Found in the pocket of a winter coat. Purchased at 7:12 in the morning. The buyer did not remember the price.**

I found the receipt strangely affecting. So much of a life is made from events that refuse to become stories. A purchase occurs. A door closes behind us. Someone says a sentence we do not quite hear. A train crosses a bridge somewhere in the distance. Nothing seems important at the time, and then the years gather those unremarkable minutes into a life we barely recognize.

The receipt knew nothing about the person who bought the coffee. It did not know whether they were happy, lonely, rushing, or exhausted. It did not know that they had stood at the counter in a fluorescent shop, trying to make a decision about the day.

But it knew they had been there.

That was enough. A receipt is a record without an explanation. It confirms hunger, payment, daylight, a transaction completed before the day became complicated. Most of our documents are designed to survive us without remembering us. A receipt is a tiny legal witness to the fact that, on one ordinary morning, a person needed coffee.

It is also a portrait made from the absence of everything else.

## The Chipped Bowl

The chipped bowl was white, with a blue line around its rim. The chip was no larger than a fingernail, but it had changed the way the bowl could be held.

You had to turn it slightly. You had to keep your thumb away from the damaged place.

The label identified its previous owner but gave no biography. It had been used for cereal, soup, and, on one occasion, a small collection of screws. It had survived two moves and one unsuccessful dishwasher. The chip had appeared when it was dropped in a sink while somebody was trying to answer the telephone.

I liked the bowl immediately.

There is a kind of perfection that makes an object difficult to love. It has no awkward angles, no difficult history, no point at which the hand has to adjust. A flawless bowl belongs to an imagined life in which nothing is ever dropped while the telephone rings.

The chipped bowl seemed more trustworthy.

Its flaw made it present. A new bowl is a possibility. A chipped bowl is a companion. Its damage is evidence of use, and its usefulness is the reason it survived.

We often speak about repairing broken things as though repair were merely the restoration of an earlier condition. But the repaired thing is not the same object it was before. A bowl with a chip is not less itself than a new bowl. It is more specific. It is the bowl that has a place for the thumb to avoid.

The museum displayed the damage under a small light, not as a tragedy but as a fact. The object had not failed to remain a bowl. It had simply become a bowl with a past.

## The Stone That Was Warm

The stone that had been warm was grey, smooth on one side, and approximately the size of a plum.

The label said it had been picked up beside a path, carried in a coat pocket for two days, and then placed in a drawer where it remained for six years.

Someone had wondered whether the warmth meant anything. The museum’s label did not say. It gave only the weather: bright afternoon, no cloud cover, stone in direct sunlight.

There was nothing mysterious about the explanation. Sunlight warms surfaces. The stone had stored a little heat and released it slowly. The person carrying it had not been holding a message from the earth or a secret source of power.

But the explanation did not undo the memory.

I know this because I once carried a warm stone home from a winter walk, though I was young enough to think the discovery might be significant. By the time I reached the house, the stone had cooled. I put it on a windowsill anyway, waiting for it to become warm again.

It never did.

What remained was not the heat but the fact of having believed, briefly and privately, that ordinary things might be more than ordinary.

The museum did not insist on the mystery. The stone was not labeled a relic. It was simply a stone that had once been warm, and someone had thought it worth keeping.

That is often how memory works. It does not preserve the sensation exactly. It preserves the fact that the sensation happened. The stone becomes proof not of the sun’s heat, but of your own attention.

## The Bus Ticket

The bus ticket was printed on thin pink paper.

The route number was clear. The time was clear. The destination was not especially memorable. The ticket had been kept for years, not because the journey had been significant, but because the person had been in the habit of keeping things.

That happens to all of us. We save objects whose importance is no longer practical. A ticket from an uneventful trip. A receipt from a shop we have closed. A key from a lock that no longer exists. We keep them not as records but as permissions.

The ticket allowed its owner to say, *I went somewhere.*

It did not say what happened there.

I tried to imagine the person who had preserved it. Probably they had looked out of the window and thought they would remember the landscape. Probably they had been tired, or distracted, or listening to music. The journey had probably passed in a series of ordinary fragments: a red car, a pedestrian crossing, a patch of sky between buildings, the driver slowing at an intersection.

When they arrived, the view was gone. Only the ticket remained.

That is a strange kind of souvenir. It gives no evidence of the place, only of the passage between one place and another. Yet we sometimes need those passages more than destinations. A life is not made entirely of arrivals. Much of it is spent in transit, looking out, thinking nothing in particular, becoming someone slightly different from the person who boarded.

The ticket was labeled:

**A journey remembered as a general feeling of movement.**

The unsent letter was written on blue paper.

It began:

**Dear—**

The name had not been entered. Or perhaps it had been entered and then erased. The label did not say.

The letter continued for half a page. Its language was apologetic but not quite submissive. It mentioned something the writer had done, something they had failed to do, and something they had decided not to explain. The final sentence was unfinished.

The museum displayed it in an envelope with a clear window, so visitors could read the first few lines without being tempted to read the rest.

Some unsent letters are apologies. Some are explanations. Some are attempts to maintain a connection after one person has already begun to let it go. They may be generous, dishonest, frightened, proud, or all four at once.

An unsent letter is a place where the past can remain unfinished.

Writing it provides a shape for feelings that might otherwise remain formless. The writer can say the sentence, revise it, cross out the more dramatic version, and decide what not to reveal. The letter is a rehearsal with no audience.

To send it would be to hand the decision to someone else. Their silence, anger, forgiveness, or indifference would enter the story and make it impossible to revise.

I do not think unsent letters are necessarily noble. They can be acts of avoidance. They can preserve a version of events that only the writer was willing to accept. But even an avoidance reveals something. It shows the distance between what we feel capable of saying and what we believe we are allowed to say.

The label beside the envelope read:

**The recipient never knew.**

A recording played the low rumble of an engine, the hiss of brakes, and the occasional announcement in a voice too indistinct to understand.

The window showed the museum behind the glass: the chipped bowl, the stone, the small lights above the cases. In front of it, it showed my face.

For a moment, the reflection made me look older. Not because it lied, but because I was looking for signs of the person I had been.

The face in the glass floated over the exhibits. Buildings passed through it. A streetlight crossed one cheek and disappeared.

The city outside was full of people whose lives I could not imagine. A woman waited at a corner. A man carried a bag of vegetables. Two children argued over a broken umbrella. I saw them as silhouettes, gestures, temporary arrangements of movement.

I invented stories about them. A person who looked certain was probably uncertain. A person who looked distracted was perhaps thinking about a parent, a debt, a forgotten message. A person who looked untroubled might be carrying the heaviest thing of all.

Then the bus in the recording passed, and the reflection changed.

That was the useful part. The city allowed me to imagine strangers without pretending to know them. For a few minutes, every person became a possible novel. But the glass also reminded me that I was doing the imagining. I could not read the stories hidden behind their faces.

A city is a place where lives overlap constantly and intimacy remains optional.

We pass one another without asking permission. We borrow the same air. We share benches, pavements, queues, crossings, and silence. The arrangement is almost perfect: close enough to notice, distant enough to remain alone.

## The Smell of Rain on Concrete

One room had no object in the center.

A window was open. The floor was slightly damp. The label on the wall read:

**AFTER THE RAIN: ONE STREET, NO DATE**

The room smelled of wet pavement, soil, leaves, and distant exhaust. It was not a strong smell. It was almost gone by the time I entered. But after a few minutes, I began to notice it.

Rain has a public smell and a private one. To one person it may mean coolness. To another, illness. To someone who has just come home, it may mean relief. To a child, it may mean being allowed to go outside. To a person in a hospital, it may mean a world continuing without them.

The smell of rain is never only the smell of rain.

It carries the memory of other storms. It brings back an apartment with leaking windows, a schoolyard, a road after a long journey, a funeral, a first kiss, a summer afternoon that seemed too bright to last.

The museum did not provide an explanation. It allowed the rain to become specific without becoming universal.

I stood in the room while the smell faded. I could not tell whether the rain had happened that morning, years ago, or only in the imagination of the person who had opened the window.

That uncertainty was part of the exhibit.

## The Light Switch That Failed

The light switch was mounted on a small wooden panel.

It did not work properly.

Turning it once produced nothing. A pause, followed by a second click, brought on the light.

The label said:

**It worked only after we had already accepted that it might not.**

I tried it several times. The ritual was oddly satisfying. Turn. Wait. Click.

Many objects in our lives are less straightforward than the diagrams that describe them. Doors stick. Cars make unfamiliar noises. Appliances require a sequence of movements that no manual has adequately explained. A drawer opens only when lifted and pulled. A machine works after being restarted. A person responds differently depending on when we ask.

We become skilled not only by learning how things function, but by learning how they resist us.

The repaired switch was more satisfying than a perfect one because its success included the method. A perfect switch asks for nothing. A troublesome one creates a small conversation between the hand, the object, and the moment.

There are lives that offer this kind of conversation more often than others. Some people require us to be patient, specific, or gentle. Some situations reward persistence. Others are simply wrong, and no amount of persistence will make them suitable.

The museum did not draw a moral lesson from the switch. It simply demonstrated that failure and familiarity can occupy the same object.

## The Bread Bag

The bread bag was brown paper, rolled shut at the top and tied with a short piece of string.

It still smelled faintly of bread.

The label explained that it had once carried a loaf home, then been emptied, folded, and reused to hold a sandwich. Its future had been modest: a lunchbox, a lining for a drawer, a place to gather small pieces of paper.

The bag was not impressive. It was not even clean. But it had participated in a life.

Bread moves through a sequence of transformations. It begins in a field, passes through hands, ovens, shops, kitchens, and tables. A bag is only one stage, but it is a necessary one. It is the temporary home between the bakery and the person who will eat what is inside.

I took the phrase personally, though I do not know why. Perhaps because the museum seemed to value not only what had been kept, but what had been given a second purpose.

A thing does not need to become valuable to become worth saving. Sometimes it is enough that it can still serve.

The label said:

These interpretations are not necessarily accurate. They are not supposed to be accurate. They are reminders that the world contains more forms than our categories can comfortably hold.

The cloud had not been a rabbit. It had also not been merely a cloud. For a few minutes, it had been a rabbit-shaped cloud, seen by one person on one afternoon.

The label added:

**The original cloud was gone within minutes. The rabbit lasted much longer.**

The label explained that the lane had once been lined with willow trees. They had been removed during a road improvement project. The official sign had remained, as had the local name.

A street can outlast the thing for which it was named. A building can become a neighborhood. A neighborhood can become a memory. A person can disappear while the street continues to receive deliveries, footsteps, arguments, rain, and sunlight.

Names are small acts of authority. They tell us how a place has been classified before we arrive. They may preserve a history, conceal one, or preserve both at once.

A willow tree is an ordinary thing. A road is an ordinary thing. Together, they can become a name that people use without thinking, a shorthand for a route they know by heart.

The museum displayed the sign beside a photograph of a road with no trees visible.

**The road is not a blank space. It is a place where several histories overlap without agreeing.**

I liked the idea of a street surviving its own explanation. It suggested that places are not entirely determined by their names, even when we inherit the names.

## The Alarm Heard Through a Wall

A small speaker produced a harsh electronic tone.

The label said:

**5:40 A.M.  
Heard through a hotel wall.  
The person who heard it was not required to wake up.**

The tone repeated three times, paused, and repeated again. It was not a pleasant sound. It was not a profound sound. It was the sound of another person’s obligation entering my attention.

At 5:40 in the morning, a person in the next room was trying to begin a day. They had an appointment, a shift, a train to catch, or a child to get ready. I did not know which. The alarm told me only that the day had started somewhere else before it started for me.

There is a strange intimacy in hearing another person’s alarm through a wall. It tells you that your private morning is not entirely private. Somewhere nearby, a body is rising. A hand is reaching for a phone. A day is being assembled from fatigue and obligation.

We do not need to know the details in order to be affected by them. The sound of someone else’s alarm makes the room feel larger. It reveals the unseen arrangement of other lives.

Most of what we call our own time is also shared time. We wake because clocks tell us to. We work when other people expect us to. We buy food because somebody has grown it, transported it, or placed it on a shelf. We sleep beside people whose dreams we will never know.

The alarm continued, insistent and ordinary.

I began to think of all the mornings that had begun as disturbance to somebody else.

## The Key With No Known Lock

The last object was a brass key.

It was not old in any impressive way. It was not marked with a famous name. It had no known lock.

The label said:

**Kept in a drawer after a move. No current use. Retained in case.**

A key is a promise made by the future to the past.

It says that some door may still exist somewhere: in a former apartment, in a forgotten bag, in the hands of someone who has not yet moved into the place where it belongs.

Keeping an unusable key is often called sentiment, as though sentiment were simply an inefficiency. But the key is also a reminder of possibilities we have not yet exhausted. The past is not entirely closed because we no longer have access to it.

I have kept keys to places I can no longer enter. I have kept them after the locks were changed, after the people had moved, after the reasons for possession had disappeared. The key no longer opens anything, but it still performs its original gesture.

It suggests that the world may contain a door we have not found.

A museum of almost nothing needs a few doors that do not open. They prevent the collection from becoming too comfortable. The exhibits are not all memories of what we have. Some are reminders of what we might still need.

## Leaving the Museum

When I left, the street looked exactly as it had before.

A car was parked beneath a tree. Someone was carrying groceries into a restaurant. The bus I had originally intended to take was still due, though its arrival had become less certain. The pavement was drying after rain. A man was arguing politely with a woman about a plan for the evening. A child was trying to step into every puddle while an adult pretended not to notice.

Nothing in the street had become more beautiful.

That was one of the museum’s quieter revelations. Attention does not improve the world in the way a fresh coat of paint improves a wall. It changes the relationship between the world and the person looking.

A chipped bowl is not transformed by being admired. The receipt does not become more significant because it has been placed beneath a light. The street sign does not suddenly reveal its history to every passerby. The objects remain what they are.

But we become less efficient at overlooking them.

The museum had not taught me a new vocabulary of wonder. It had not given me a method for finding meaning in everything. Many of its exhibits were too ordinary to support such a claim. The bread bag was a bread bag. The key was a key. The alarm was an alarm.

That was precisely the point.

We use the word *ordinary* as though it meant unimportant. But ordinary can also mean familiar, open, available, unpretentious. It can describe the things that have not been elevated by distance or rarity. The person beside us. The food on our plate. The sound of a door closing. The route we take every morning. The name of a street remembered by someone who will never see it again.

Most of what we will love will first become ordinary.

A song becomes ordinary after enough repetitions. A face becomes ordinary when we no longer need to study it. A room becomes ordinary once we know where the light falls and which floorboard complains. Love often begins not with astonishment but with familiarity. We do not fall in love with a face that remains entirely mysterious. We fall in love with the face we begin to expect, and then continue to see more clearly.

The habit of noticing is not the same as the habit of finding everything extraordinary. It is gentler than that. It allows a thing to remain small while still deserving attention.

A receipt can be a record of a morning. A chipped bowl can hold a history. A bus ticket can preserve the fact of movement. An unsent letter can contain a whole unresolved life. A street can carry a vanished tree. A key can keep the shape of a door in the imagination.

These things do not solve the major questions. They do not explain why we are here or what happens after we leave. They do not make the city more manageable or the past more recoverable.

They make the present harder to waste.

Outside, the day continued without announcement. The clouds did not resemble anything in particular. The bus was late. The groceries were probably going to spoil if they were left in the car. Someone nearby was about to make a mistake, recover from it, and continue.

I stood on the pavement for a moment longer than necessary.

The museum had given me no object. There was no miniature bowl in my pocket, no key, no blue-paper letter. I had entered with a collection of things I would have discarded and left with the uncomfortable awareness that I had been discarding them for years.

That was the only exhibit I could not put back in its case.

The admission had been one thing you were going to throw away. Mine was a receipt, folded twice, carrying a coffee ring and a price I could no longer remember paying.

For a long time afterward, I did not know what to do with it.

Then one ordinary morning, while waiting for the kettle, I unfolded it.

The date was still there. The total was still there. The name of the shop had faded almost completely, but the paper proved that the purchase had happened, even if the person who made it could not remember why.

I put it back in my pocket.

The museum had been right about at least one thing. Most of life disappears before it has a chance to become a story.

The receipt knew less than I did.

Still, it was enough to prove that I had been there.

One room had no object in the center.

**AFTER THE RAIN: ONE STREET, NO DATE**

Rain has a public smell and a private one. To one person it may mean coolness. To another, illness. To someone who has just come home, it may mean relief. To a child, it may mean being allowed to go outside. To a person in a hospital, it may mean a world continuing without them.

The smell of rain is never only the smell of rain.

It carries the memory of other storms. It brings back an apartment with leaking windows, a schoolyard, a road after a long journey, a funeral, a first kiss, a summer afternoon that seemed too bright to last.

I stood in the room while the smell faded. I could not tell whether the rain had happened that morning, years ago, or only in the imagination of the person who had opened the window.

That uncertainty was part of the exhibit.

## The Light Switch That Failed

The light switch was mounted on a small wooden panel.

It did not work properly.

Turning it once produced nothing. A pause, followed by a second click, brought on the light.

The label said:

**It worked only after we had already accepted that it might not.**

I tried it several times. The ritual was oddly satisfying. Turn. Wait. Click.

Many objects in our lives are less straightforward than the diagrams that describe them. Doors stick. Cars make unfamiliar noises. Appliances require a sequence of movements that no manual has adequately explained. A drawer opens only when lifted and pulled. A machine works after being restarted. A person responds differently depending on when we ask.

We become skilled not only by learning how things function, but by learning how they resist us.

The bread bag was brown paper, rolled shut at the top and tied with a short piece of string.

It still smelled faintly of bread.

The label explained that it had once carried a loaf home, then been emptied, folded, and reused to hold a sandwich. Its future had been modest: a lunchbox, a lining for a drawer, a place to gather small pieces of paper.

The bag was not impressive. It was not even clean. But it had participated in a life.

There was an empty case beneath a framed photograph of the sky.

The label said:

The photograph showed a broad grey-white cloud with a rounded edge. I could not see the rabbit. I looked for several minutes before finding it: two soft projections, a suggestion of ears, the possibility of a face.

Once I saw it, I could not stop seeing it.

The rabbit was not hidden by poor photography. It was produced by the mind’s willingness to find a pattern where none had been intended.

We tend to imagine that imagination is a force for making things unlike reality. In practice, it often works by making reality more particular. It takes a shape and offers a story. A cloud becomes a rabbit. A stain becomes a map. A stranger’s expression becomes a warning or an invitation.

The label added:

The final room contained a metal street sign.

It read:

**WILLOW LANE**

The label explained that the lane had once been lined with willow trees. They had been removed during a road improvement project. The official sign had remained, as had the local name.

A street can outlast the thing for which it was named. A building can become a neighborhood. A neighborhood can become a memory. A person can disappear while the street continues to receive deliveries, footsteps, arguments, rain, and sunlight.

I liked the idea of a street surviving its own explanation. It suggested that places are not entirely determined by their names, even when we inherit the names.

## The Alarm Heard Through a Wall

A small speaker produced a harsh electronic tone.

The label said:

**5:40 A.M.  
Heard through a hotel wall.  
The person who heard it was not required to wake up.**

The tone repeated three times, paused, and repeated again. It was not a pleasant sound. It was not a profound sound. It was the sound of another person’s obligation entering my attention.

At 5:40 in the morning, a person in the next room was trying to begin a day. They had an appointment, a shift, a train to catch, or a child to get ready. I did not know which. The alarm told me only that the day had started somewhere else before it started for me.

There is a strange intimacy in hearing another person’s alarm through a wall. It tells you that your private morning is not entirely private. Somewhere nearby, a body is rising. A hand is reaching for a phone. A day is being assembled from fatigue and obligation.

We do not need to know the details in order to be affected by them. The sound of someone else’s alarm makes the room feel larger. It reveals the unseen arrangement of other lives.

Most of what we call our own time is also shared time. We wake because clocks tell us to. We work when other people expect us to. We buy food because somebody has grown it, transported it, or placed it on a shelf. We sleep beside people whose dreams we will never know.

The alarm continued, insistent and ordinary.

I began to think of all the mornings that had begun as disturbance to somebody else.

## The Key With No Known Lock

The last object was a brass key.

It was not old in any impressive way. It was not marked with a famous name. It had no known lock.

The label said:

**Kept in a drawer after a move. No current use. Retained in case.**

A key is a promise made by the future to the past.

It says that some door may still exist somewhere: in a former apartment, in a forgotten bag, in the hands of someone who has not yet moved into the place where it belongs.

Keeping an unusable key is often called sentiment, as though sentiment were simply an inefficiency. But the key is also a reminder of possibilities we have not yet exhausted. The past is not entirely closed because we no longer have access to it.

I have kept keys to places I can no longer enter. I have kept them after the locks were changed, after the people had moved, after the reasons for possession had disappeared. The key no longer opens anything, but it still performs its original gesture.

It suggests that the world may contain a door we have not found.

A museum of almost nothing needs a few doors that do not open. They prevent the collection from becoming too comfortable. The exhibits are not all memories of what we have. Some are reminders of what we might still need.

## Leaving the Museum

When I left, the street looked exactly as it had before.

A car was parked beneath a tree. Someone was carrying groceries into a restaurant. The bus I had originally intended to take was still due, though its arrival had become less certain. The pavement was drying after rain. A man was arguing politely with a woman about a plan for the evening. A child was trying to step into every puddle while an adult pretended not to notice.

Nothing in the street had become more beautiful.

That was one of the museum’s quieter revelations. Attention does not improve the world in the way a fresh coat of paint improves a wall. It changes the relationship between the world and the person looking.

A chipped bowl is not transformed by being admired. The receipt does not become more significant because it has been placed beneath a light. The street sign does not suddenly reveal its history to every passerby. The objects remain what they are.

But we become less efficient at overlooking them.

The museum had not taught me a new vocabulary of wonder. It had not given me a method for finding meaning in everything. Many of its exhibits were too ordinary to support such a claim. The bread bag was a bread bag. The key was a key. The alarm was an alarm.

That was precisely the point.

We use the word *ordinary* as though it meant unimportant. But ordinary can also mean familiar, open, available, unpretentious. It can describe the things that have not been elevated by distance or rarity. The person beside us. The food on our plate. The sound of a door closing. The route we take every morning. The name of a street remembered by someone who will never see it again.

Most of what we will love will first become ordinary.

A song becomes ordinary after enough repetitions. A face becomes ordinary when we no longer need to study it. A room becomes ordinary once we know where the light falls and which floorboard complains. Love often begins not with astonishment but with familiarity. We do not fall in love with a face that remains entirely mysterious. We fall in love with the face we begin to expect, and then continue to see more clearly.

The habit of noticing is not the same as the habit of finding everything extraordinary. It is gentler than that. It allows a thing to remain small while still deserving attention.

A receipt can be a record of a morning. A chipped bowl can hold a history. A bus ticket can preserve the fact of movement. An unsent letter can contain a whole unresolved life. A street can carry a vanished tree. A key can keep the shape of a door in the imagination.

These things do not solve the major questions. They do not explain why we are here or what happens after we leave. They do not make the city more manageable or the past more recoverable.

They make the present harder to waste.

Outside, the day continued without announcement. The clouds did not resemble anything in particular. The bus was late. The groceries were probably going to spoil if they were left in the car. Someone nearby was about to make a mistake, recover from it, and continue.

I stood on the pavement for a moment longer than necessary.

The museum had given me no object. There was no miniature bowl in my pocket, no key, no blue-paper letter. I had entered with a collection of things I would have discarded and left with the uncomfortable awareness that I had been discarding them for years.

That was the only exhibit I could not put back in its case.

The admission had been one thing you were going to throw away. Mine was a receipt, folded twice, carrying a coffee ring and a price I could no longer remember paying.

For a long time afterward, I did not know what to do with it.

Then one ordinary morning, while waiting for the kettle, I unfolded it.

The date was still there. The total was still there. The name of the shop had faded almost completely, but the paper proved that the purchase had happened, even if the person who made it could not remember why.

I put it back in my pocket.

The museum had been right about at least one thing. Most of life disappears before it has a chance to become a story.

The receipt knew less than I did.

Still, it was enough to prove that I had been there.
